tier_reason: README Benchmarks table gives first-party RTX 3090 timings against e3nn, and public scripts exist (benchmarks/bench_spherical_harmonics.py times e3nn.o3.spherical_harmonics with CUDA events; benchmarks/benchmark_e2e_mace.py has an e3nn per-op breakdown). No compiler flags or host CPU are stated, and not every README row has a matching baseline script, so C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (RTX 3090, N_atoms=1000, C=32, ~20 neighbours/atom): spherical harmonics L=3 0.142 ms (e3nn) vs 0.012 ms (11.8x); tensor product 1.847 ms vs 0.089 ms (20.8x); TP backward 3.21 ms vs 0.156 ms (20.6x); fused SH+TP 0.574 ms vs 0.413 ms (1.39x), listed under an 'e3nn (baseline)' column, but the matching script benchmarks/benchmark_fused_sh_tp.py only compares fused against batmobile's own unfused SH+TP+scatter pipeline, so that row appears to be fused vs unfused batmobile rather than vs e3nn. At N_atoms=5000, C=64, ~30 neighbours: fused 5.935 ms vs unfused batmobile 8.604 ms (1.45x).
corrections.caveats: Small project (44 stars, 3 commits, all dated 2026-01-17 and co-authored with Claude), first-party numbers from one GPU with no compiler flags or host CPU. Baseline is the generic e3nn, not an optimised library such as cuEquivariance or OpenEquivariance. Benchmark scripts do not back every README row: the README names benchmarks/benchmark_tensor_product.py, which does not exist (raw fetch 404); benchmarks/benchmark_tp_backward.py times only batmobile (no e3nn baseline; timing via time.perf_counter over 100 launches); benchmarks/benchmark_fused_sh_tp.py compares fused vs batmobile's unfused pipeline, not e3nn, although the README places its 1.39x row under the e3nn column. Only the spherical-harmonics script and the end-to-end MACE script time e3nn directly. Covers L_max=3 only.

notes: Metadata confirmed via github.com page: MIT (LICENSE 'Copyright (c) 2025 Batteries Authors'), 44 stars, 7 forks, not archived, not a fork, 3 commits all on 2026-01-17. Shortcoming to record: README row 'Fused SH+TP' attributed to e3nn is backed by a fused-vs-unfused batmobile script; README-named TP benchmark script is missing.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: BitBLAS is the library form of Ladder, a peer-reviewed OSDI'24 paper whose artifact (branch osdi24_ladder_artifact of this repo, scripts under artifact/Figure12 and artifact/Table1, CUDA 12.0 Dockerfile) benchmarks against cuBLAS, cuDNN, CUTLASS and vLLM on an A100-80GB-PCIe; the paper-result Figure 12 image was opened. Host CPU and compiler flags are not stated and the paper PDF (usenix.org) was blocked, so B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: W_INT2 A_INT8 GEMV/GEMM '8x/2x speedup over cuBLAS W_FP16 A_FP16 on A100' (shown only in the op_benchmark_a100_int2_scaling image). benchmark/README.md: on RTX 3090, FP16 and INT8 Tensor Core GEMM 'matches the performance of cuBLAS and CUTLASS'; float16xnf4 GEMV/GEMM 'achieves 2x the speed of bitsandbytes and 4x the base float16 performance'; on A100, int4 dequantize 'outperforms bitsandbytes, faster-transformer, tensorrt-llm, vLLM, and Marlin'. Ladder OSDI'24 Figure 12 (artifact/Figure12/paper_result/operator_performance_a100.png, A100, approximate bar readings normalised to Ladder's own FP16 kernel): at equal FP16 precision cuBLAS is roughly at parity (about 0.85x to 1.3x of Ladder FP16, i.e. cuBLAS is faster on some GEMM shapes); Ladder W_INT4 A_FP16 reaches about 3.5x and W_INT1 A_INT8 about 10x over Ladder FP16 on the largest GEMM shapes; on the 8 convolution shapes cuDNN sits at roughly 0.1x to 0.75x of Ladder FP16. A WebSearch summary of the paper (PDF not opened) also cites average 1.8x over cuBLAS for W_FP16 A_FP16 and 4.5x for W_INT1 A_INT8, up to 13.3x on V100 and 14.6x on A6000; these could not be checked against the text.
corrections.caveats: The 8x/2x figure compares W_INT2 A_INT8 against a W_FP16 A_FP16 cuBLAS GEMM, so the gain comes largely from moving fewer bytes, not from an equal-precision kernel; at equal FP16/INT8 precision the repo only claims to match cuBLAS/CUTLASS, and the paper's Figure 12 shows cuBLAS at rough parity (faster on some shapes). Result plots are images; figure values are bar readings. The peer-reviewed numbers are for the Ladder artifact branch (TVM/Welder-based compiler, CUDA 12.0), not the later TileLang-based BitBLAS release. Repo archived 2026-02-24; last commit 2025-05-05. cuBLAS is not one of the category baselines; cuDNN appears only in the paper's convolution panel. Third-party baselines in benchmark/README.md are reproduced via the separate LeiWang1999/mlc-benchmark repo (not opened).

notes: Metadata confirmed via github.com: MIT (Microsoft), 770 stars, archived 2026-02-24, not a fork, last commit 2025-05-05 ('Update tilelang&cutlass to newest (#303)'), so abandoned is right. Ladder paper venue confirmed by README citation (OSDI 24) and the artifact branch README; usenix.org PDF EGRESS_BLOCKED, so paper numbers come from a WebSearch snippet only.

tier_reason: README tables give first-party mean/max speedups over KernelBench PyTorch eager, torch.compile and CUDA Graph references on five GPUs, with per-task code and scores released in optimized_cuda_code/*.json; no software versions, flags or host CPU, and the released data do not support the headline maximum, so C with the claim corrected.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README A100 table: mean 3.12x (median 1.42x, max 120x) vs Default (KernelBench eager reference); vs Torch Compile mean 2.77x (median 1.72x); vs Torch Compile RO 2.88x (median 1.67x); vs CUDA Graph 2.81x (median 1.20x, 25th percentile 0.954x, faster than the CUDA Graph reference in only 147 of 229 tasks). Mean speedup vs Default by GPU: A100 3.12x, 3090 2.51x, H100 3.85x, H20 2.38x, L40 3.13x. The released optimized_cuda_code/a100.json gives score_default mean 3.05x, median 1.40x, geometric mean 1.76x, max 110.8x over 241 scored tasks (derived from page data); its score_cudnn field (reference run with cuDNN backend flags) has median 1.87x over 236 tasks (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The headline mean and max are driven by degenerate KernelBench tasks, not faster kernels. In the released A100 file the top task (level 2 task 83, score 110.8x) has custom_code that performs the same conv3d, GroupNorm, min, clamp and dropout as the reference (a code comment says 'Only the standard path remains after removing caching'), so the 110.8x score cannot come from the released code; the task's output is identically zero. Level 2 task 80 (31.3x) returns a cached zero tensor and monkeypatches __class__.__call__ because the reference output is always zero for that shape; level 1 task 12 (65x) rewrites diag(A) @ B as a broadcast multiply in PyTorch. By a simple text check only 85 of 241 released A100 solutions contain custom CUDA code (load_inline or __global__); the rest are PyTorch-level rewrites. The README itself reports RL reward hacks (extra CUDA streams to fool timing, result caching); a WebSearch summary of later papers reports that most top-10 solutions use no custom CUDA kernel and that filtering contaminated tasks drops the mean from 3.13x to 1.49x (source pages not opened). Not a reusable library: per-task generated snippets. No software versions, flags or host CPU. Baselines are naive eager PyTorch, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen.

notes: Claim overstated: headline 120x/3.12x rests on degenerate zero-output tasks and a top score whose released code equals the reference (correctness/measurement problem worth recording; consider wrong category since output is RL-generated per-task PyTorch snippets, not a library).
